card.thesis: Same mechanism as round 1: a Bollinger squeeze (band width under 8% of price) marks a name where buyers and sellers have reached a temporary truce, and a close back above the upper band out of that compression is the market resolving the truce in one direction, which systematic trend-following flow (CTAs, momentum funds, dealer hedging) then chases -- so a minority of breaks turn into extended continuation moves while the majority are false starts. The counterparty on a losing trade is whoever sold the breakout expecting immediate mean reversion and was right only briefly. What changes in round 2 is the universe and, because of it, the stop and the honesty about how thin the edge is. I redid the MAE stop study (my most careful round-1 work) on this cross-asset roster: across 1,367 squeeze-release signals on SPY/XLU/XLP/TLT/EFA/EEM/IBB/KRE/GDX (2003-2026 history, sma(20)-break-or-60-day exit, no stop), 0.0% of eventual winners ever retraced 4% or more from entry before their real exit -- the worst winner MAE in the whole sample was -3.9%. In round 1's semiconductor/AI universe a 5% stop cut over a quarter of eventual winners; here even a 3% stop only clips 0.4% of them. ETFs compress and release in smaller, shallower moves than single stocks, so I tightened the stop from round 1's 8% to 5% -- it costs essentially no winners here and meaningfully caps the loser tail, which single-stock-calibrated 8% would have left unnecessarily wide. I also checked the specific regime that broke the round-1 version: in round 1's universe, 2022 was 0% win rate across 5 trades, all in one correlated sector. On this diversified roster, 2022 produced 24 signals across 8 different symbols (XLU, XLP, SPY, TLT, EFA, EEM, IBB, KRE, GDX) at a 54.2% win rate and +0.79% mean return -- the semiconductor selloff that killed every round-1 signal simply didn't touch defensive sectors, long bonds, or EM equities compressing and releasing on their own schedules. That is the actual case for this round-2 card: not a stronger raw edge, but survival of a regime that was fatal to the concentrated version. I have to report the honest cost of that survival, though: aggregate profit factor across this roster is only ~1.00-1.04 (mean winner ~3.2%, mean loser ~-1.9%, win rate ~37%), roughly stable across sma-exit periods 15-30 and hold windows 40-90, versus round 1's ~1.35 on the same mechanism applied to higher-volatility single names. Diversification bought regime survival at the price of a much thinner raw edge -- close to breakeven before any transaction costs -- because ETF breakouts simply don't travel as far as single-stock breakouts. I measured correlations before assuming them: TLT/SPY correlation is 0.07 over the trailing 5 years (vs -0.31 over the full 2002-2026 history, a real regime shift toward positive stock-bond correlation since 2022's inflation shock) and GDX/SPY is 0.18-0.45 depending on window -- both genuinely low, which is the diversification this card is trying to buy. GDX earns its slot on that low correlation despite contributing 5 of the worst 10 trades in the entire sample from just 2% of signal count -- its squeezes are rarer (27 signals vs 100-236 for the others) and its releases gap harder than anything else in the roster, which the previous-close/next-open stop mechanic cannot fully contain.
card.entry: (bb_upper(20,2) - bb_lower(20,2)) < close * 0.08 and close crosses_above bb_upper(20,2)
